newsitem.title: QATAR: Qatar sees higher spending, revenue in 97/98 budget.
newsitem.headline: Qatar sees higher spending, revenue in 97/98 budget.

text.p: The Gulf Arab state of Qatar on Sunday forecast higher spending and revenue in its 1997/98 budget and vowed to work towards its economic goals of wiping out a deficit and developing its oil and gas income.

A Finance Ministry statement, carried by the official Qatari news agency, projected higher spending of 16.38 billion riyals ($4.5 billion) and increased revenue of 13.39 billion with a slightly higher deficit of 2.98 billion.
It said the budget runs from April 1.
The 1996/97 deficit was 2.95 billion riyals on spending of 13.75 billion and revenue of 10.80 billion.
Qatar's 120,000 citizens enjoy one of the world's highest per capita incomes of $22,000 per year and until the early 1980s the state registered a cash surplus.

But massive investments in projects to develop the North Field -- the largest single reservoir of natural gas in the world -- and create new sources of revenue have caused balance of payment deficits in recent years.

The statement did not say what oil price the budget was based on, but Energy and Industry Minister Abdullah bin Hamad al-Attiyah said on March 19 Qatar would base its 97/98 budget at $16 a barrel of oil, up 40 cents from the last financial year.
Qatar, a member of the Organisation of Petroleum Exporting Countries (OPEC), receives about 70 percent of its state revenues from oil sales and the rest from energy-based industries.

In the 1997/98 financial year, Qatar coffers will be boosted by higher oil output and revenues from its Qatargas liquefied natural gas (LNG) plant. Qatar in December started its first LNG exports and officials hope that would help shore up the economy.
Analysts said the 24.1 percent increase in projected revenue in the 97/98 budget would largely be based on projections of higher oil prices and increased oil, condensate and gas output.
Qatar produces around 550,000 barrels per day (bpd) of crude oil and has the world's third largest reserves of gas after Russia and Iran.
The statement said the budget was part of government plans to wipe out the deficit by the year 2000, diversify the economy and increase public income.

"The financial problems we are facing will not last long, as they are by nature linked to the remaining time needed to complete our basic projects, some of which have started to bear fruit," the statement added.

The International Monetary Fund has forecast that Qatar's oil and gas exports will more than double annual public income to $7 billion by the year 2000. It said in coming years the income growth would mainly come from natural gas exports which would result in the "elimination of any fiscal deficit by the year 2000."

The Finance Ministry said Qatar would press ahead with its economic priority to develop oil and gas revenue and "work to provide the needed financial resources to cover the expenses of big productive projects especially in oil, gas and infrastructure sectors".
It said it will also work to develop the private sector.

It said 1.2 billion riyals were allocated in the new budget to public services and infrastructure projects and 1.1 billion to economic activities like building a new airport in Doha at a cost of 413.8 million riyals.
